1. Core Clinical Tension: A 20-year-old male presented with chronic draining scalp sinuses, an upper eyelid sinus, progressive painless globe dystopia, proptosis, and extradural cranial invasion following remote forehead trauma. Mycetoma typically affects the feet or lower extremities (Madura foot); cephalic and orbital dissemination is exceptionally rare and can easily be misdiagnosed as orbital cellulitis, fungal osteomyelitis, or an aggressive orbital neoplasm. The presence of sinuses discharging characteristic granules provides the pivotal clinical sign.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Admission triage concludes after documenting presentation of chronic discharging sinuses and traumatic laceration history, ophthalmic exam (dystopia, 2 mm proptosis, left gaze restriction, eyelid swelling with discharging sinus), scalp exam showing sinus tracts draining white grains, and routine laboratory work (leukocytosis), immediately prior to microbiological culture, histopathology, CT, and MRI.
3. Differential Distinctions: Eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma) was in the differential for chronic grain-discharging sinus disease, but microbiological isolation and staining demonstrated Gram-positive branching bacterial filaments rather than fungal hyphae. Orbital neoplasm was considered given progressive painless dystopia, proptosis, and extradural invasion, but excluded by granulomatous suppurative inflammation with grain extrusion.
case_prompt:
A 20-year-old male presented to an ophthalmology clinic with complaints of multiple draining sinus tracts over the scalp for one year. He noted a concurrent discharging sinus over the left eyelid for one year, accompanied by painless, gradually progressive displacement (dystopia) of the left eyeball for six months, without diplopia or reduction in visual acuity. Five years prior, he had sustained a fall onto his left forehead resulting in a lacerated wound over the left eyebrow that had been sutured.

On ocular examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. The right eye was normal. Examination of the left eye revealed globe dystopia measuring 20 prism diopters downwards and 10 prism diopters outwards on prism bar testing, and exophthalmometry demonstrated relative proptosis of 2 mm in the left eye. Extraocular movements were preserved except for restriction in left gaze. The left upper eyelid exhibited diffuse soft tissue swelling with an active discharging sinus tract. Anterior segment, pupillary reactions, fundoscopy, and diplopia charting were normal. Examination of the scalp revealed multiple chronic sinus tracts actively draining purulent fluid containing visible white grains.

Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable except for peripheral leukocytosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Primary orbital neoplasm / Invasive skull base tumor
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to chronic, progressive painless globe displacement, proptosis, and extradural cranial extension; ruled out by presence of suppurative draining sinus tracts and Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon on biopsy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Histopathology revealed lympho-histiocytic infiltration with focal abscess formation. Inset shows an eosinophilic granule exhibiting a Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon with a background of neutrophils [Fig. 5].

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as a leading cause of chronic sinus tracts with macroscopic grain discharge; excluded by microbiologic demonstration of branching actinomycete bacilli rather than fungal hyphae.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Microbiology testing of the erosive scalp and lid lesions showed pus cells and Nocardia Asteroides / Nocardia Brazilensis bacillus, highly suggestive of actinomycetoma.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Microbiological examination of the scalp and eyelid sinus exudates demonstrated pus cells and Nocardia asteroides / Nocardia brasiliensis bacilli, and histopathology confirmed actinomycotic granules with Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon, confirming orbital and scalp actinomycetoma.

editor_comments: A rare presentation of cranio-orbital actinomycetoma involving the scalp, upper eyelid, and orbit with extradural extension following remote forehead trauma, successfully treated with a combination of streptomycin, cotrimoxazole DS, and rifampicin.
